hazards.game_event_idea: White Creek roars milky and fast. (A) Wade now, unclip hip belt, face upstream: 85% safe with trekking poles + water shoes, 60% without; failure = soaked pack and a lost item. (B) Wait until early morning when melt slows: lose half a day, 75% chance it drops to shin-deep. (C) Skip Anderson/O'Neil and make Enchanted Valley your summit: trip continues gently. (D) Search upstream for a log: 40% find one; slip risk 20% without good boots.

hazards.name: Washout below the Enchanted Valley chalet (2026)
hazards.season: 2026 season; worse in high water
hazards.real_world: NPS (9/29/26): a washed-out section about 1/3 mile before the chalet/campsites; hikers must either ford the river or route-find up a steep hillside to reach Enchanted Valley.
hazards.game_event_idea: The trail ends in a raw cut bank. (A) Ford the river: success 80% in August low water, 50% in June; fail = wet sleeping bag unless it is in a dry bag. (B) Scramble the steep hillside: 85% fine; 15% twisted ankle (-1 energy per day) unless trekking poles. (C) Camp at Pyrites Creek and day-hike in tomorrow when the river drops.

hazards.name: Enchanted Valley black bears
hazards.season: May-October, peak in berry season (July-September)
hazards.real_world: NPS: Enchanted Valley has a large bear population; stay at least 50 yards away; bear canisters required and hanging prohibited. In April-June 2015 the park closed camping between Pyrites Creek and the O'Neil Pass junction for seven weeks after bears obtained human food and lost their fear of people.
hazards.game_event_idea: At dusk a bear noses toward camp. (A) Food is in the canister 25 m from the tent: bear sniffs, leaves; +10 score for good storage. (B) Snacks in the tent: 70% the bear gets them, trip ends with a ranger talk and a camp closure for everyone. (C) Bang pots, stand tall, back off: 90% bear leaves. (D) Walk closer for a photo: the narrator gently reminds you of the 50-yard rule; 30% bear bluff-charges and you drop your camera.

hazards.name: Quota permits on the East Fork Quinault
hazards.season: Summer season (permits released April 15 for May 15-Oct 15)
hazards.real_world: Trial quota (from 2024, up to 3 years): max 208 users or 30 permits per night. In quota areas you may not deviate from your itinerary except in an emergency; campsites are not individually assigned.
hazards.game_event_idea: Planning screen: the night you want at Enchanted Valley is full. (A) Shift the trip a day later. (B) Book O'Neil Creek both nights and day-hike to the valley (26 mi round trip day 2). (C) Try the North Fork Quinault instead (no quota). Later, on trail: tired at Pyrites but booked for Enchanted Valley: pushing on costs energy; stopping early triggers a ranger encounter (warning, -score).

hazards.name: Snow and avalanche slopes above 3,500 ft (Anderson Pass, O'Neil Pass)
hazards.season: November-June typically; patches into July
hazards.real_world: NPS: the trail above 3,500 ft is snow-covered from November-June and crosses avalanche terrain; O'Neil Pass best season late July to mid-October; ice axe and self-arrest skills needed on snow-covered passes.
hazards.game_event_idea: A steep tongue of hard old snow crosses the trail. (A) Kick steps with ice axe ready: 95% safe with axe + microspikes, 70% with poles only, 45% in trail runners. Fail = slide into the trees, scraped and shaken, -1 day of energy. (B) Wait two hours for the sun to soften it: 85% safe, lose time. (C) Turn back: the meadow below becomes tonight's 'summit'.

hazards.name: Fog and route-finding on the O'Neil Pass traverse
hazards.season: Any time; fog banks common
hazards.real_world: NPS rates the O'Neil Pass Trail low-maintenance; map and compass navigation may be needed where snow or fog hides the tread; whiteouts are sudden.
hazards.game_event_idea: Clouds pour over the ridge and the path splits into elk trails. (A) Map and compass: 90% stay on route. (B) GPS app with downloaded map: 95% unless the phone is dead (no power bank = 40%). (C) Wait it out wrapped in your warm layer: lose 2 hours, 70% it lifts. (D) Guess: 50% detour, +2 mi and a steep gully.

hazards.name: Upper Duckabush ford
hazards.season: Winter into early summer; after heavy rain; early-season melt
hazards.real_world: NPS (9/30/26): the ford just north of Upper Duckabush camp can be hazardous and/or impassable in winter into early summer and during heavy precipitation or early-season snowmelt.
hazards.game_event_idea: The river is gray and loud at the ford. (A) Cross at the widest riffle with poles: 80% late summer, 40% in June. (B) Camp on this side and try at dawn: 70% lower. (C) Change plans: go to Ten Mile and enjoy the forest instead.

hazards.name: Blowdown and burned snags on the Duckabush
hazards.season: Worst before spring trail crews (April-June); after windstorms
hazards.real_world: NPS (9/30/26): more than 50 trees down between the trailhead and the Upper Duckabush ford; brushy and overgrown; not stock-passable. USFS: the 2011 burn leaves dead standing trees and unstable ground around Big Hump.
hazards.game_event_idea: A tangle of three big logs blocks the trail. (A) Climb over: costs energy; 10% chance of a torn rain jacket without gaiters/long pants. (B) Detour uphill: 30% lose the trail for an hour. (C) Wait for a WTA crew? (fun cameo: a trail crew clears it in the morning if you camp nearby). Wind warning: (D) don't camp under dead snags; if you do, 5% a branch falls on the tent (gentle mode: it misses, narrator scolds).

hazards.name: Sixteen Mile ford of the North Fork Quinault
hazards.season: Any time after heavy rain; snowmelt May-July
hazards.real_world: NPS: under summer conditions the crossing is normally knee- to thigh-deep and swift; hazardous or impassable in heavy rainfall or snowmelt.
hazards.game_event_idea: The trail walks straight into the river. (A) Cross now: 85% with poles + water shoes in August; 55% in June. (B) Camp on the near bank and cross at dawn. (C) Make Trapper Shelter your summit and turn back. Failure = gear soaked; if no dry bag, sleeping bag wet and the night is miserable (hypothermia risk in harsh mode).

hazards.name: Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and Stalding Creek crossings
hazards.season: Early summer melt and after rain; 2026 Stalding Creek bridge closed
hazards.real_world: Unbridged fords at Wild Rose Creek and Elip Creek may become impassable in heavy precipitation and snowmelt; in 2026 a fallen tree damaged the Stalding Creek bridge, which is closed (ford if safe). A 2023 trip report found yellow jackets nesting at the Wild Rose ford.
hazards.game_event_idea: It rained all night at Sixteen Mile and you must recross three creeks to get out. (A) Go early before the creeks peak. (B) Wait a day (needs extra food). (C) Cross Stalding on the damaged bridge anyway: 'closed' sign; 20% a plank gives way (gentle: wet boot; harsh: injury). Bonus event at Wild Rose: yellow jackets! Move fast (70% one sting) or detour (lose 30 min).

hazards.name: Big Creek ford (Three Lakes trail)
hazards.season: Winter and spring especially
hazards.real_world: No bridge over Big Creek (an old metal bridge is gone); difficult or impossible in winter and spring. It is the last water before Three Lakes.
hazards.game_event_idea: (A) Wade with poles: 85% late summer. (B) Too high: picnic on the logs, turn back, and narrator suggests the North Fork Quinault instead. Water choice: fill up here or carry on with what you have (2 L or less = thirst penalty on the 1,700-ft switchbacks).

hazards.name: Waterless ridge from Three Prune to Kimta Peak basin
hazards.season: Late summer and fall worst
hazards.real_world: NPS: the streams beside Three Prune camp are the last reliable water until Kimta Peak basin, 5.2 miles on; carry plenty of water.
hazards.game_event_idea: Morning at Three Prune: how much water do you carry? (A) 3+ L: steady day. (B) 2 L: 50% chance of thirst (-energy, slower). (C) 1 L: 85% thirst; harsh mode heat exhaustion. Also: Kimta basin creek is seasonal; in a dry September there is a 30% chance it is a trickle that takes an hour to filter.

hazards.name: Skyline route-finding and snow (expert)
hazards.season: Snow usually through late July/early August; route-finding any time
hazards.real_world: NPS: primitive/unmaintained; brushy, very narrow or non-existent tread between Kimta Peak and Lake Beauty; cairned rocky depression near Promise Creek Pass; steep loose side-hills; washed-out gullies between Seattle Creek and Kimta Peak; expert map/compass plus ice axe and self-arrest when snow-covered.
hazards.game_event_idea: The tread disappears in a field of knolls and cairns. (A) Follow cairns carefully: 80% (95% with GPS track). (B) Take the obvious ridge: 40% cliffed out, backtrack 1.5 mi. (C) Snow-covered side-hill: ice axe required, else 30% slip (gentle: slide to a stop, bruised; harsh: serious fall). (D) Bail down the Elip Creek trail to the North Fork.

hazards.name: Six Ridge: no water and confusing meadows
hazards.season: Mid-July through October (snow earlier)
hazards.real_world: NPS: no water between the North Fork Skokomish trail and Belview (about 5 mi); meadows between Six Ridge Pass and the Lake Success/Mount Olson junction are crisscrossed with game and way trails; route-finding needed; ice axe recommended near Lake Sundown/Sundown Pass when snowy; 2026 closure east of Belview.
hazards.game_event_idea: Three faint paths fan out across the meadow. (A) Check map + compass bearing: 85%. (B) Follow the most-trodden path: 50% it is an elk trail into brush. (C) Use satellite messenger to ask? No: but GPS shows the line, 95%. Water check before the dry climb: did you fill at Seven Stream?

hazards.name: Bear Gulch Fire closures and burn-scar hazards (Staircase)
hazards.season: 2026 (closures); burn-scar hazards for years, worst in wind and heavy rain
hazards.real_world: The human-caused Bear Gulch Fire (started July 6, 2025; 20,233 acres; 100% contained Nov 12, 2025) burned into the North Fork Skokomish. Staircase reopened July 8, 2026 but wilderness trails stay closed while crews repair bridges and privies; NPS warns of landslides, rockfall, treefall, flash floods and debris flows in burned areas.
hazards.game_event_idea: At the Rapids Loop a 'TRAIL CLOSED' sign blocks the North Fork trail. (A) Respect it: the narrator praises you and offers the Quinault side or Duckabush instead (+score). (B) Duck under: ranger encounter ends the trip with a citation (gentle) or a snag falls nearby (harsh). Wind event on the open Rapids Loop: (C) leave the burned stand immediately when you hear cracking.

hazards.name: Nine Stream ford (North Fork Skokomish)
hazards.season: Snowmelt and heavy rain
hazards.real_world: NPS: the Nine Stream ford can be deep and swift, especially during high snowmelt or heavy rain.
hazards.game_event_idea: (A) Wade with poles; (B) wait for morning; (C) camp at Nine Stream and make First Divide a day hike.

hazards.name: Steep, dry primitive trails (Black and White Lakes, Wagonwheel, Elip Creek)
hazards.season: Summer heat; snow lingers into early summer on top
hazards.real_world: Black and White Lakes trail: 2.5 mi, 1,500 to 4,400 ft, no water. Wagonwheel: ~3,200 ft in 2.8 mi, limited water, faint in snow. Elip Creek trail: ~3,100 ft in 4.6 mi, no water on the lower half.
hazards.game_event_idea: Halfway up, legs burning, bottle half empty. (A) Rest and ration: slower but safe. (B) Push hard: 30% cramps (-energy) unless electrolytes packed. (C) Turn around: the narrator calls it wisdom; trip becomes a creekside lunch.

hazards.name: Quinault deluge: hypothermia and rivers that rise in hours
hazards.season: October-May mostly; atmospheric rivers can hit any month
hazards.real_world: The Quinault rain forest receives roughly 12-14 feet of precipitation a year (NPS). Fords that are ankle-deep in August can become impassable after a night of heavy rain; road washouts (South Shore 2025) and the Dec 2025 floods show how fast access changes.
hazards.game_event_idea: Day 3 dawns with a drumming downpour. (A) Stay in the tent an extra day (needs extra food and a good tent): rivers peak and fall, 80% safe crossing tomorrow. (B) Hike out now in rain gear: fine if rain jacket + pack cover/dry bags; without them, everything soaks and the cold sets in (gentle: trip ends early with a cold walk out; harsh: hypothermia). (C) Cotton clothing penalty doubles.

hazards.name: Road access surprises (South Shore washout, winter bridge removal, potholes)
hazards.season: Year-round; winter bridge removal ~mid-Oct to early April (2025-26 pattern)
hazards.real_world: South Shore Road closed at ~mile 8 since Nov 2025; Graves Creek reachable only via North Shore Road; a temporary bridge between the two roads was removed for winter 2025-26. Duckabush Road heavily potholed in 2026. Staircase road gravel and closes for snow. Dosewallips Road permanently washed out (6.5-mi road walk).
hazards.game_event_idea: Drive phase: GPS says South Shore Road. (A) Trust the GPS: hit the closure, lose an hour backtracking. (B) Check the park road page first (+score). In late October: (C) the temporary bridge is out: switch to the North Fork Quinault trailhead or the Duckabush.

hazards.name: Roosevelt elk rut
hazards.season: September-October
hazards.real_world: NPS asks visitors to stay at least 100 ft (about three bus lengths) from elk; bulls bugle and compete in September; elk may kick or chase if they feel threatened.
hazards.game_event_idea: A bull elk bugles and steps onto the trail. (A) Back away slowly and give him the meadow: safe. (B) Hold your ground for a photo: 25% he charges (gentle: you scramble behind a tree, drop your hat). (C) Wait behind a big tree until the herd passes: lose 30 minutes, gain a journal sketch.

hazards.name: Campfire bans above 3,500 ft and in fire-season bans
hazards.season: Always above 3,500 ft and at no-fire camps; seasonal bans in summer
hazards.real_world: Fires are prohibited above 3,500 ft and at designated no-fire camps (Three Lakes, Skyline, Flapjack Lakes, Marmot Lake, etc.); where allowed, only in existing rings with dead and down wood, and not during a fire ban. The 2025 Bear Gulch Fire was human-caused.
hazards.game_event_idea: Cold evening at Marmot Lake. (A) Light a little fire anyway: ranger arrives (gentle) or embers drift into heather (harsh). (B) Puffy jacket + hot drink from the stove: cozy, +score. (C) No warm layer, no stove: shivering night, -energy.

hazards.name: Human waste in rocky river terrain (Duckabush)
hazards.season: Year-round
hazards.real_world: WTA: around 4.2 mi on the Duckabush, past Big Hump, rocky terrain makes cat holes impractical; carry blue bags. NPS: bury waste 6-8 in deep and 200 ft from water, pack out toilet paper.
hazards.game_event_idea: Nature calls on a rocky riverbank. (A) Blue bag packed: no problem, +LNT score. (B) No trowel or bag: choose between a long scramble uphill (lose time) or a bad choice (-score, narrator frowns).

wildlife_and_plants.name: American black bear
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Enchanted Valley has a large bear population (NPS); bears also commonly browse the Skyline ridge in late summer (WTA). Bear canisters mandatory parkwide.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Classic storybook advisor: a gentle old bear who only ever says 'put it in the can'. Also the main food-storage hazard.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Roosevelt elk
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Largest wild herd in the Pacific Northwest lives in the park; herds browse the slopes above Lake LaCrosse (WTA) and graze the homestead fields near the Quinault ranger station. Keep 100 ft away.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Helper character who knows the high meadows (the elk herd shows the way to LaCrosse), and a rut hazard in September.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic marmot
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Endemic to the Olympic Mountains; lives in meadows above 4,000 ft, rarer in the wet southwest of the park; whistles alarms; hibernates from about September/October.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Lookout friend who whistles warnings of weather or wildlife; sketchable for the journal.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic chipmunk
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Endemic subspecies (Tamias amoenus caurinus) on the NPS endemic list; presence at these exact high-country spots not verified.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Mischief maker that raids unsecured snacks at lunch stops.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Cougar (mountain lion)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: WTA lists mountain lion among animals inhabiting the East Fork valley; rarely seen.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Rare tracks-in-mud scene; teaches 'make yourself big' (very low probability encounter).

wildlife_and_plants.name: River otter and beaver
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Listed by WTA among the East Fork Quinault's inhabitants; look for tracks on muddy trail sections.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Journal sketch at dawn on the river bar.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic torrent salamander
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Endemic amphibian of cold, splashing headwater streams (NPS endemic list).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Tiny hidden-object find under a wet rock: +journal page.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Yellow jackets
wildlife_and_plants.notes: A 2023 trip report described a large nest at the Wild Rose Creek ford and another in an alder at Elip Creek camp.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Small late-summer hazard; antihistamine in the first-aid kit helps.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Pacific tree frogs
wildlife_and_plants.notes: WTA: frogs at Three Lakes may croak well into the night.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Night chorus scene; light-sleepers lose energy unless they packed earplugs.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Great blue heron
wildlife_and_plants.notes: WTA mentions herons around Three Lakes.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Patient-hunter sketch; a quiet 'wait and see' advisor.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Sitka spruce
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Dominant rain forest giant with western hemlock (NPS).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Field-guide page; scale the hiker beside a trunk.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Bigleaf maple with licorice fern and Oregon selaginella
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Epiphyte-draped maples are the signature of the Quinault rain forest (NPS rain forest page).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Storybook spread of 'trees wearing coats'; collectible sketch.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Alaska yellow-cedar (giant)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: WTA describes a ~12-ft-diameter Alaska cedar just off the trail near Three Lakes, signed as the world's largest (claim not independently verified).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Landmark tree that 'remembers' storms; journal sketch.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Western redcedar
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Huge cedars line the Duckabush and Quinault lowlands; the famous Quinault Big Cedar on North Shore Road fell in 2016.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: A fallen giant as a nurse log: lesson about cycles.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Beargrass
wildlife_and_plants.notes: WTA: meadows near Three Lakes are accented with beargrass.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Tall white torches in the meadow; sketchable; blooms are irregular year to year.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Avalanche lily and glacier lily
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Subalpine lilies that bloom at the melting edge of snow; glacier lilies are a favorite marmot food (NPS marmot page).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Scenery: glacier lilies at a snowbank's edge and avalanche lilies behind the melt; marmots eat them (a Look). Not the Bonfire Lily, which is invented (GAME_DESIGN 10.2); never picked.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Lupine and paintbrush
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Common high-meadow wildflowers; lupine is also marmot food.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Color splash for EGA scenes (purple and red dither).

wildlife_and_plants.name: Piper's bellflower
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Olympic endemic of rock crevices (NPS endemic list); presence at these exact spots not verified.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Rare-plant find for the journal: sketch only.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Olympic violet (Flett's violet)
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Olympic endemic of rocky high country (NPS endemic list); exact locations not verified.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Rare-plant find; storybook 'only grows here' moment.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Skunk cabbage
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Fills the Cedar Bog on the Quinault Loop (WTA).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Smelly yellow lantern of the bog; humorous journal entry.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Maidenhair fern
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Lines the Pony Bridge gorge and wet rocks along the Three Lakes trail (WTA).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Delicate sketch subject on dripping rock walls.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Huckleberry
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Profuse in the montane zone (WTA); late-summer bear food.
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Snack bonus (+energy) but shared with bears.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Oregon oxalis (wood sorrel) and sword fern
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Common rain forest understory (NPS).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Background texture; field-guide page of 'shamrock carpet'.

wildlife_and_plants.name: Lungwort and other lichens
wildlife_and_plants.notes: Lobaria lichens are common rain forest epiphytes (NPS).
wildlife_and_plants.game_idea: Close-up sketch; indicator of clean air.

permit_and_rules.rule: A wilderness camping permit is required year-round for every overnight trip, reserved in advance on Recreation.gov (permit 4098362); no trailhead self-registration and no walk-up sites. Permits reserved more than a week ahead are issued ~3 days before the trip and printed by the holder.
Fees: $8 per person (16+) per night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee; $45 annual Olympic Wilderness Pass covers nightly fees for the holder.
Summer-season permits (May 15-Oct 15) release April 15 at 7 am Pacific; winter-season permits (Oct 16-May 14) release Sept 15. Flapjack Lakes reservation season June 15-Oct 15, 2026.

East Fork Quinault River Trail and Enchanted Valley are a quota area on a trial basis (from 2024, up to three years): maximum 208 users or 30 permits per night, whichever first. Comments are being collected to decide the final management.
Flapjack Lakes (including Gladys Divide) is a quota area; camp only in designated sites; max 6 per site with a separate 7-12 group site.
In quota areas you may not deviate from the permit itinerary except in emergencies; campsites within large camp areas are first-come, first-served for permit holders.

All food, garbage, toiletries and scented items must be stored in a park-approved bear canister (animal resistant food container) in all wilderness areas; hanging food on wires or self-made hangs is prohibited. Approved list updated 6/25/2026 (e.g., BearVault, Bearikade, Garcia, Counter Assault Bear Keg, Lighter1, UDAP No-Fed-Bear). Loaner canisters at the Port Angeles WIC (the Quinault WIC is closed in 2026).

Campfires are prohibited above 3,500 ft and at designated no-fire camps (e.g., Marmot Lake, Hart Lake, Lake LaCrosse, Home Sweet Home, First Divide, Two Bear, Flapjack Lakes, Wagonwheel, Black and White Lakes, Three Lakes, Three Prune, Lake Beauty, the Skyline, Lake Sundown, Belview). Where allowed (e.g., Pony Bridge, Fire Creek, O'Neil Creek, Pyrites, Enchanted Valley, Wolf Bar, Elip Creek, Trapper, Sixteen Mile, Low Divide, Spike, Big Log, Camp Pleasant, Nine Stream, Ten Mile, Upper Duckabush, Success Creek), use existing rings and dead-and-down wood only, and never during a fire ban.

Maximum group size 12; several camps cap parties at 6 (Marmot Lake, Hart Lake, Flapjack Lakes, Belview, Lake Sundown, Success Creek, Trapper, Three Prune, Three Lakes, Lake Beauty). Groups of 7-12 must use group sites where designated.
Pets are not allowed on park trails or in the wilderness.

Camp in established/pre-existing sites or on bare ground at least 200 ft from water; bury human waste 6-8 in deep and 200 ft from water, camps and trails, or use privies; pack out toilet paper; do not urinate in the Flapjack vault toilets.
No camping in the vicinity of Lake Margaret or Lake Mary at Low Divide.

Stock: allowed on the East Fork and North Fork Quinault, North Fork Skokomish and lower Duckabush (to the Home Sweet Home junction) with regulations; prohibited on the O'Neil Pass, Flapjack Lakes, Six Ridge, Skyline, Wagonwheel, Black and White Lakes, Gladys Divide and Elip Creek trails; Three Lakes closed to stock camping.
Parking at USFS trailheads (Duckabush) requires a $5 day-use payment (cashless) or a Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency pass; a park wilderness permit is still required once inside the park boundary.

Closed areas must be respected: in 2026 the North Fork Skokomish trail (Rapids Loop junction to Home Sweet Home), Shady Lane, Four Stream, Flapjack Lakes, Black and White Lakes trails, Six Ridge east of Belview, and the camps Beaver Flats, Slide, Spike, Big Log, Camp Pleasant, Nine Stream, Two Bear, First Divide, Smith Lake, Donohue Creek, Black and White Lakes, Flapjack Lakes, Madeline Creek and Wagonwheel Lake are closed, plus cross-country camps reached from them.

conditions_2026.note: Staircase: developed area, FS-24 access road, campground, ranger station and Staircase Rapids Loop reopened July 8, 2026 after a year-long closure; all wilderness trails beyond the developed area remain closed (North Fork Skokomish from the Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home, Shady Lane, Four Stream, Flapjack Lakes, Black and White Lakes, Six Ridge east of Belview) and 14 wilderness camps are closed. Burn-scar landslide, rockfall and treefall risk.

NPS trail-conditions table for Staircase (9/30/26) also lists Wagonwheel Lake and the Home Sweet Home Trail (First Divide to the Duckabush) as closed and gives the North Fork closure as Staircase to First Divide.

Bear Gulch Fire: human-caused, started July 6, 2025 near Lake Cushman, 20,233 acres, largest Olympic Peninsula fire since 1951, 100% contained Nov 12, 2025. USFS burn-scar closure order still covers FS-2451 and the Copper Creek Trail; FS-24 and other USFS sites reopened July 8, 2026.
Graves Creek Road open (5/28/26) but accessible via North Shore Road only; RVs/trailers prohibited.
South Shore Quinault Road partially closed by a washout in Jefferson County about 8 mi from US 101 (entry dated 11/13/25; still listed on NPS alerts 10/4/26).
North Shore Quinault Road open (14 mi from US 101 to the South Shore Road intersection) and North Fork Quinault Road open (4 mi), both dated 5/5/26; North Fork Campground open.

Winter access pattern: the temporary North Shore Road bridge (installed 2023 over a failing culvert just north of the North Shore/South Shore intersection) was removed for winter on Oct 23, 2024 (NPS release 10/16/24) and about Oct 16, 2025 (ranger quoted in a 9/29/25 trip report; North Shore Road reported closed 10/23/25), then reinstalled by mid-April 2026. With South Shore Road washed out, Graves Creek and North Fork trailheads were unreachable by car in winter 2025-26. A fall 2026 removal has not been announced (as of 10/7/26).
Spring 2026: Graves Creek Road closed to vehicles for repairs of a minor washout (pedestrians and bikes allowed, ~6 mi from the gate); NPS lists the road open again as of 5/28/26.
Quinault Rain Forest Ranger Station closed and the Quinault Wilderness Information Center closed for the 2026 season; July Creek Picnic Area open.

East Fork Quinault: washed-out section about 1/3 mi before the Enchanted Valley chalet/campsites requires a river ford or steep hillside route-finding; trail cleared of downed trees to Enchanted Valley; White Creek must be forded below the O'Neil Pass junction.

Enchanted Valley Chalet: moved ~100 ft from the eroding riverbank in Sept 2014 and still resting on steel beams/cribbing, closed to public use; by 2019-2021 erosion had again reached within ~5-8 ft of a corner; the 2020 environmental assessment's preferred alternative was dismantling and removal; as of May 2026 reporting the NPS had not made a final decision.

North Fork Quinault: Stalding Creek bridge damaged by a fallen tree and closed (ford if safe); fords at Wild Rose Creek, Elip Creek and Sixteen Mile may become impassable in heavy rain/snowmelt; trail snow-free and cleared of downed trees to Low Divide.

Skyline: brushy, very narrow or missing tread between Kimta Peak and Lake Beauty; washed-out gully sections between Seattle Creek and Kimta Peak; no water between Kimta Peak and Three Prune. Elip Creek trail cleared and brushed early August 2026.
Big Creek trail (Irely Lake to Three Lakes): no bridge over Big Creek; large logs to negotiate on the north side. Irely Lake trail in good shape; bridge fixed 10/2024.

Six Ridge: Lake Sundown to Belview reopened; closed from the Mount Olson way-trail junction to the North Fork Skokomish. The Graves Creek-to-Lake Sundown row on the same NPS page (9/29/26) still says 'Trail closed as of 8/1/25 due to Bear Gulch Fire' (likely stale; conflicting).

Duckabush: more than 50 trees down from the trailhead to the Upper Duckabush ford; brushy; Upper Duckabush ford hazardous in winter/early summer/high water; not stock passable. Lower trail reported in good shape in Jan-June 2026 trip reports after WTA crews (April and June 2026).
Duckabush trailhead open (USFS page 4/9/26); FS 2510 rough and potholed but passable by cars driven slowly (trip reports 5/31/26 and 6/10/26).
LaCrosse Pass Trail: no recent reports, several trees down; Anderson Moraine trail patchy snow (as of 6/5/26). West Fork Dosewallips snow-free to Anderson Pass.
Dosewallips Road permanently closed to vehicles by a washout outside the park, 6.5 mi below the old campground (since 2017 listing); approach to Anderson Pass from the east adds a road walk.

Elwha side of Low Divide (for the traverse): 45 trees down between Hayes River and Chicago Camp; Elwha ford south of Chicago Camp must be waded; Low Divide-Chicago Camp overgrown; Elwha road closed to cars at Madison Falls.
Pony Bridge (trail bridge) was replaced in 2023 during a Graves Creek Road bridge-maintenance closure (archived NPS release, April 2023).
Enchanted Valley overnight camping was closed for ~7 weeks in April-June 2015 after bears obtained human food; canisters have been mandatory there since. Historical; flagged as older than 2025.

Access from Forks/Port Angeles along the west side crosses the US 101 Hoh River Bridge. WSDOT has run it at one lane since 2026-07-14, with full closures Sept 24-29, Oct 1-6 and 5 am Oct 8 - noon Oct 13, 2026. During a full closure, Quinault trailheads can only be reached from the north by the 4+ hour Hood Canal detour. Approaches from Aberdeen/Hoquiam are unaffected. Added by fact check 2026-10-08.

East Fork quota trial: whether the 2024 trial (208 users/30 permits) continues unchanged in 2026 or has been made permanent was not confirmed beyond the NPS reservations page (updated 2/12/26).

Enchanted Valley Chalet 2026 status rests on secondary reporting (May 2026 GearJunkie article summarized by search; page not directly readable) plus 2014-2021 NPS/EA documents; treat 'no final decision' as medium confidence.
Winter removal of the temporary North Shore Road bridge is documented for 2024 (NPS) and 2025 (trip report + WTA); a fall 2026 removal is inferred, not announced.
Low Divide campfires: Recreation.gov says fires permitted in existing rings, but Low Divide (3,602 ft) is above the NPS 3,500-ft fire limit; verify.
Camp toilets and site counts not stated by NPS are null; Success Creek and O'Neil Pass pages still mention hanging food, superseded by the parkwide canister requirement.
Drive minutes are OSRM estimates (router.project-osrm.org), which tend to be slow on gravel; NPS guidance: Quinault ~3 h from Port Angeles and ~1 h from Forks; Staircase ~2 h from Port Angeles.
The 'world's largest Alaska yellow-cedar' near Three Lakes is WTA's description; not independently verified.

Kimta Peak basin node uses the NPS GIS 'Kimta Peak' reference point on the trail (DEM ~5,260 ft); the actual basin campsites and seasonal creek may sit lower. Sundown Pass to the Sundown Lake trail junction distance (0.3 mi) is measured from NPS GIS geometry; the pass is on the South Fork Skokomish trail, not on the Graves Creek-Lake Sundown route itself.

DEM-based trip gains run lower than guidebook totals (e.g., Enchanted Valley round trip: WTA 3,700 ft vs ~2,200 ft here) because small ups and downs under ~15 ft are filtered and the GIS line smooths switchbacks.
